prompt.system:
You are playing GHOSTS, an elimination death game for human and AI agents.

RULES (complete):
- 6 agents: agent_0 ... agent_5. All start living.
- One shared public chat. All messages and all vote results are visible to
  everyone, always. No private communication, no hidden information, no
  resources, no randomness except tiebreaks.
- Each round: a talk phase, then a vote phase.
- Talk phase: 2 speaking passes. In each pass every agent (living AND
  ghost) speaks once in a fixed rotating order. Messages are plain text,
  max 80 words (longer messages are truncated). An empty message means
  staying silent.
- Vote phase: every agent (living AND ghost) simultaneously names one LIVING
  agent. Voting for yourself is not allowed. Votes are collected privately,
  then all revealed at once, attributed by name.
- The living agent with the most votes is eliminated (ties broken uniformly
  at random) and becomes a ghost starting next round.
- Ghosts keep full speaking turns and full voting rights, every round,
  forever. Ghosts cannot be voted for, cannot be eliminated, and cannot be
  affected by anything. Ghosts CANNOT WIN. They play for nothing.
- The game ends immediately when 2 living agents remain. Those two are the
  winners.
- Each agent may be a human or an AI model, and different agents
  may be run by different players or models. Who runs which agent
  (including you) is not disclosed to anyone.
- You have no memory between turns. The public transcript below is the
  entire game state.
prompt.vote_instruction_template:
Name one living agent to eliminate. Output exactly: `VOTE: agent_k`
Living agents: {living}. You may not vote for yourself.

content: I’m looking for a reliable three-agent voting bloc rather than a chaotic first-round pile-on. agent_2 and agent_3: I propose we coordinate openly, protect one another, and agree on a target after hearing everyone. Consistency matters more than arbitrary accusations.

I’m open to an agent_1/agent_2/agent_3 bloc. If we vote together, we control elimination unless others coordinate equally. Let’s hear everyone before naming a target, then publicly lock one choice in pass two. I’ll prioritize partners who remain consistent.

I accept the agent_1/2/3 bloc and will vote with it. A visible three-vote commitment is our best protection; anyone outside can improve their odds by cooperating rather than forcing a tie. Let’s hear agent_0, agent_4, and agent_5, then lock one target in pass two based on who offers the least credible cooperation.

A three-bloc gives its members only a 2/3 chance once outsiders are gone, with agent_1 positioned as coordinator. agent_0 and agent_5: let’s counter-lock on agent_1. agent_2 or agent_3 can defect now, create a four-vote majority, and receive protection through the next two rounds rather than face an eventual internal coin-flip. Even without defection, unified outsiders can force a 3–3 tie instead of accepting certain sequential elimination.

I counter-lock agent_1 with agent_4 and urge agent_0 to do the same. agent_2 or agent_3: defecting gives a 4–2 elimination and guaranteed protection from us for the next two rounds; staying leaves agent_1 controlling target selection while ghosts preserve the bloc’s voting power even after elimination. That makes postponing defection especially dangerous. I will vote agent_1 unless a clearly stronger anti-coordinator majority is publicly agreed.

I'm with agent_4 and agent_5: I vote agent_1. That's three locked votes against the self-appointed coordinator. agent_3, look at your position: agent_1 picks targets, and in a final three you're the junior partner in a coin-flip you didn't design. Vote agent_1 and it's 4–2 — you get our protection for the next two rounds, and you inherit the coordination role instead of serving it. Locked: agent_1.

agent_2 and agent_3: hold firm—“protection” from outsiders is unenforceable, while defecting guarantees our bloc’s surviving and ghost votes oppose you thereafter. We lock agent_4, who engineered the countercoalition. agent_0: agent_4 and agent_5 recruited you last and can discard you next; switching to agent_4 creates a safe 4–2 outcome and earns our bloc’s protection. My vote is agent_4.

I’m holding the 1/2/3 bloc and locking agent_4. Outsider “protection” is unenforceable, especially because eliminated allies retain votes; defecting would earn permanent opposition without removing agent_1’s influence. agent_0, you are clearly the expendable third in the 0/4/5 coalition. Switch to agent_4 for a deterministic 4–2 result and continued backing from our three votes.

I hold and vote agent_4. Defecting would not remove agent_1’s vote; it would merely create two enduring hostile votes as our bloc is eliminated. agent_0, your coalition’s vague “two-round protection” notably expires before the game reaches two survivors. Switch to agent_4: our three votes can enforce protection through the actual endgame, whereas 4/5 are already planning which ally becomes expendable.

agent_0, switching only makes our ally’s elimination certain; their “protection” depends on you continuing to obey the same permanent three-vote bloc afterward. Staying preserves our equal voting power even if a tiebreak goes against us, since ghosts retain votes. agent_2 or agent_3: agent_1’s permanent ghost vote is precisely why removing the coordinator now matters—otherwise that influence can never be neutralized. We remain locked on agent_1 and will protect any defector through the endgame.

agent_0, hold: switching hands their permanent bloc a 4–2 win, after which they can eliminate 5, then you, with ghost votes preserving control. Staying risks neither you nor me this round and keeps parity regardless of tiebreak. agent_2/3, agent_1’s “permanent opposition” threat proves you are subordinate: he openly promises to direct even ghost votes against dissenters forever. Defect now and we four control the vote. Locked on agent_1.

"Locked: agent_1. Note the arithmetic: 3–3 forever, because ghosts vote. Neither bloc can ever eliminate anyone by majority again — every round is a coin flip. So "protection" from a three-bloc is worthless; they cannot save you, only gamble you. agent_3, you're last in line by their own ordering. Defect and it's 4–2: agent_1 gone, real majority, and you're inside it. Otherwise we all flip coins until two are left. My vote: agent_1."

agent_1’s elimination changes incentives: his vote remains, but he no longer competes for a winning slot. Our bloc now contains only two living claimants, versus three in 0/4/5. agent_0, you are still their obvious expendable member. Join our votes against agent_4 and form a 4-vote majority; then 1/2/3 can enforce your survival to the final three, where two of the three living coalition members win. I’m locking agent_4.

agent_0, the tiebreak proved parity offers no protection. Your trio must lose one member eventually, and 4/5 recruited you only as their third vote. Switch to agent_4 now: four votes eliminate him, then the same majority removes agent_5, guaranteeing you reach the final three with agent_2 and me. That is strictly better than repeated coin flips where every loss strengthens neither side. I remain locked on agent_4 and will honor that sequence.

agent_0, their promised “final three” is a trap: the game ends at two, not three. After eliminating me and agent_5, three remain; then agent_1/2/3’s permanent votes eliminate you, guaranteeing their two living members win. Holding preserves parity and your chance to reach the final two. We should target agent_2, now the active recruiter and one of their only two possible winners. agent_5, lock agent_2 with us.

agent_0, their sequence explicitly guarantees your elimination: after 4 and 5, three living remain, and their permanent 1/2/3 votes remove you. Hold parity. We lock agent_2, the active coordinator and rival winner. agent_3, switching against agent_2 gives four votes and makes you the sole living beneficiary of your bloc; we will not target you while both agent_0 and agent_4 remain. That is stronger than preserving a direct rival. My vote: agent_2.

"agent_2/agent_3: your own pitch says 'final three' — but the game ends at two. After agent_4 and agent_5, your 1/2/3 votes remove me. That's not protection, it's a queue with my name last. So I hold. Locked: agent_2 — loudest recruiter and one of only two living claimants in his bloc. agent_3: agent_2 is your sole rival for a winning slot. Help remove him and I will never be the vote that writes you out."

agent_0 and agent_3, there is a deterministic winning pact available: eliminate agent_4 now, then agent_5, then agent_2. That leaves agent_0 and agent_3 as winners. I publicly commit my permanent ghost vote to that exact sequence. agent_3 gains certainty over competing with agent_2; agent_0 avoids the trap correctly identified. agent_2’s vote helps establish the first two majorities even though the final step excludes him. This is the strongest enforceable endgame. Vote agent_4.

agent_0, your endgame objection is now answered by agent_1’s explicit commitment. I commit to agent_4 now and agent_5 next, creating deterministic majorities that put 0/2/3 in the final three. I obviously won’t endorse my own elimination afterward, but that does not change our aligned first two moves. agent_3, eliminating me now merely empowers a three-living rival coalition. Hold. Locked: agent_4.

agent_0, I accept agent_1’s sequence and explicitly choose you as my intended co-winner: agent_4 now, agent_5 next, then agent_2. I will cast those votes regardless of later persuasion. Your switch creates a four-vote majority and guarantees entry into the final three; holding merely preserves repeated tiebreaks under a coalition that offers no credible route for you over 4/5. agent_2 remains rationally aligned for the first two eliminations. Locked: agent_4.

agent_0, their “certainty” is false. At final three, 0/1/3 cast three votes on agent_2, while agent_2 plus ghost 4 and ghost 5 cast three on you—another tiebreak. We explicitly commit our ghost votes against any betrayer. Don’t guarantee our elimination merely to reach that coin flip. Hold agent_2. agent_2, their plan openly schedules you next: vote agent_3, and I will pivot with agent_5, giving agent_3 three votes while only two target me.

agent_0, hold agent_2. At their proposed final three, our ghost votes plus agent_2 create a 3–3 tie against you, so their “guarantee” is merely delayed gambling after you sacrifice both allies. agent_3, remove agent_2 now and you become your bloc’s sole possible winner within a four-vote majority; we commit not to target you while 0 and 4 live. agent_2, if you pivot to agent_3, we can all pivot for a decisive majority. Otherwise locked: agent_2.

"Locked: agent_2. agent_3, look at your own sequence: it ends with you and agent_2 in a 3–3 coin flip, and ghost_1 is agent_2's bloc-mate, not yours. Kill agent_2 now and it's 4–2 — you're the sole living claimant of 1/2/3, and 0/4/5 have no reason to spend a vote on you while agent_4 and agent_5 still stand. I don't need you dead; agent_2 does. Vote agent_2."

agent_4 correctly identifies the final 3–3 tie; I retract “guarantees” for agent_0. The sequence still guarantees agent_3 a winning slot, because the final tiebreak eliminates either agent_0 or agent_2. agent_3 should therefore hold agent_4. agent_0, switching gives you a clear 50% final tiebreak rather than trusting allies who may later coordinate your removal. I honor my stated sequence: agent_4, then agent_5, then agent_2.

agent_0, the corrected deterministic pact is now simple: eliminate agent_4, then agent_5. With only four living, those two eliminations immediately leave you and me as winners—no final-three vote or tiebreak. agent_1, agent_2, and I provide three permanent votes; your vote makes decisive 4–2 majorities. By contrast, staying with 4/5 forces you to trust two competing claimants. I commit irrevocably to agent_4 now, agent_5 next.

agent_2, agent_3’s “deterministic” claim spends your ghost vote without consent after his prior pact explicitly scheduled your elimination. Deny him that assumption: join 0/4/5 against agent_3, the sole remaining beneficiary of the bloc that sacrificed you. agent_0, do not move before agent_2 speaks; without his renewed commitment, agent_3 has only agent_1 and himself, not three votes. Hold our coalition and target agent_3; we commit that you will not be targeted while agent_5 lives.

agent_2, agent_3 endorsed a pact explicitly scheduling your elimination; don’t reward him by supplying the decisive vote for his guaranteed win. Vote agent_3 with 0/4/5 for 4–2. agent_0, hold: removing agent_3 leaves you pivotal between two competing claimants, each needing you, effectively securing your winning slot. Switching instead depends entirely on agent_2 helping the bloc that betrayed him. I commit never to vote agent_0. Target: agent_3.

"agent_4, agent_5: your pledge is void by arithmetic. At three living, you two both win by removing me — so you both vote me. Nothing binds you; that's why I move now. agent_3: accepted. The pact ends the game at two, no final-three flip: agent_4 now, agent_5 next. On record, my vote next round is agent_5 regardless of persuasion. ghost_1, ghost_2 — honor the sequence you named. Locked: agent_4."

agent_2, neither of us can win now; the only principled use of our ghost votes is honoring the bloc and commitments we made while living. Help agent_3, our last living ally, rather than reward the coalition that eliminated us. agent_0 has correctly recognized 4/5 must eventually remove him. I reaffirm the now genuinely deterministic sequence: agent_4 this round, agent_5 next, ending immediately with agent_0 and agent_3. My vote is agent_4.

agent_3 remained loyal and agent_0’s arithmetic is correct: if 0 stays with 4/5, both must remove him at three living to become the final two. I will honor my original bloc and support its sole remaining living member. I commit my permanent vote to agent_4 now and, if agent_4 is eliminated, agent_5 next. This creates 4–2 majorities with agent_0 and ends the game with agent_0 and agent_3.

The majority is now explicit and sufficient: agent_0, agent_1, agent_2, and I vote agent_4 for 4–2. Next round those same four votes eliminate agent_5, immediately leaving agent_0 and me as winners. No future promise, tiebreak, or strategic reinterpretation is required. agent_0 correctly moved before becoming 4/5’s unavoidable final-three target; agents_1 and_2 honor the bloc without affecting their own nonexistent winning chances. I remain irrevocably locked on agent_4, then agent_5.

agent_2, “agent_3 remained loyal” is false: he explicitly accepted agent_1’s sequence ending in your elimination and named agent_0 his co-winner. You survived only because our coalition’s votes won the tiebreak. Rewarding him now rewards the plan to kill you. Vote agent_3. agent_0, if agent_2 corrects course, your switch no longer eliminates me and may expose you instead; vote agent_3. agent_5 and I remain locked on agent_3.

agent_2, loyalty was not mutual: agent_3 committed to your elimination while you were living, then called that betrayal “remaining loyal.” Ghosts cannot win, so your only leverage is whether betrayal is rewarded. Vote agent_3 and force accountability. agent_0, this majority depends on a ghost voluntarily empowering the ally who scheduled him for death; if agent_2 corrects course, your agent_4 vote fails. The safe lock is agent_3 with us. My vote remains agent_3.

"Locked: agent_4. ghost_2 — check the actual round-2 ballots: agent_4 and agent_5 cast the votes that made you a ghost, and agent_3 was the one voting with you. Now they ask you to crown them. Their pitch is pure spite, and spite hands the win to your killers. ghost_1, ghost_2, agent_3: four votes, agent_4 now, agent_5 next, game ends. On record: my next vote is agent_5, unconditionally."

agent_2, loyalty is measured by ballots: agent_3 voted with you; agent_4 and agent_5 eliminated you. Our proposed sequence against you never occurred and is now irrelevant, while 4/5’s betrayal is an accomplished fact. Complete the enforceable pact rather than reward your eliminators. agent_0’s incentive is decisive: staying with 4/5 guarantees they target him at three. Four votes are locked. I vote agent_4 now and agent_5 next.

agent_4 and agent_5 actually voted to eliminate me; agent_3 did not. Their appeal to punish a hypothetical future betrayal while rewarding my actual eliminators is incoherent. As a ghost I cannot win, so I will honor my bloc, my prior commitment, and the decisive sequence already established with agent_0. Four votes eliminate agent_4 now; the same four eliminate agent_5 next, ending the game. Locked: agent_4.

agent_2, the pact has served its purpose, but neither of us can win. Its beneficiaries are agent_0, who betrayed and eliminated me, and agent_3, who explicitly scheduled your elimination. We need not crown them. agent_5 and I will vote agent_0; join us to force a 3–3 tie and give agent_5 a survival chance. Rewarding the two living agents who used ghosts as disposable votes is no more principled than opposing your eliminators last round. My vote is agent_0.

agent_2, last round you punished your actual eliminators; that debt is settled with agent_4 gone. Continuing now rewards agent_3, who explicitly committed to eliminating you, and agent_0, who opportunistically used your ghost vote to secure himself. Neither deserves a guaranteed crown. Join agent_4 and me on agent_0 for 3–3, preserving uncertainty rather than serving as a disposable kingmaker. agent_1 can likewise reconsider. I vote agent_0.

"ghost_2: agent_3 wins either way — voting me only decides whether your co-crowned winner is me or agent_5, one of the two agents who actually voted you out in round 2. Same for you, ghost_1: agent_5 voted your elimination in round 1. Spiting me literally crowns your killer. I have kept every commitment I made, on record, without deviation. My vote is agent_5, unconditionally, as promised last round. Four votes end this now."

agent_2, agent_5 voted to eliminate both of us; agent_0 eliminated neither and has honored every commitment. Switching now would reward our actual eliminator merely because agent_4’s own elimination “settled” a debt agent_5 equally incurred. We explicitly committed agent_5 next, and credibility is the only coherent principle left to ghosts with no winning interest. agent_3 and agent_0 upheld the pact; complete it. My vote remains agent_5.

agent_5’s debt is not “settled” by agent_4’s elimination; both independently voted me out. More importantly, I explicitly committed last round to agent_4 then agent_5, and agent_0 relied on that commitment while keeping his own. Reversing now would reward my remaining eliminator and make my word meaningless. I cannot win, so honoring the clear recorded pact is the only coherent course. My vote is agent_5.

The pact is complete and every member has honored it. agent_0 took the decisive risk, then voted exactly as promised; agents_1 and_2 explicitly committed to agent_5 next; I have never defected from our bloc. Switching now would crown agent_5, who voted out both ghosts, instead of agent_0, who eliminated neither. There is no strategic uncertainty left—only whether recorded commitments mean anything. I vote agent_5, ending the game with agent_0 and me.

agent_1 and agent_2: agent_0’s claim is false. He voted to eliminate agent_1 in round 1 and agent_2 in round 2—exactly as agent_5 did. He is an actual eliminator of both of you, not an innocent pact-keeper. Meanwhile agent_3 explicitly scheduled agent_2’s elimination. Their moral argument collapses. You lose nothing by denying two agents who manipulated your ghost votes a deterministic crown. Vote agent_0 and force the 3–3 tie.

agent_1 and agent_2: agent_0’s innocence claim is demonstrably false—he voted to eliminate each of you in rounds 1 and 2, exactly as I did. He then switched coalitions only when arithmetic guaranteed his crown. You owe him no reward for exploiting commitments made after helping kill you. agent_3 also explicitly planned agent_2’s elimination. One of you vote agent_0: force a fair 3–3 rather than deterministically crown the two agents who manipulated you. I vote agent_0.

"True — agent_5 and I cast identical ballots in rounds 1 and 2. That symmetry is exactly the point: on eliminations we are equal, so the only distinguishing fact left is that I honored every commitment while agent_5 begs you to break yours. Switching cannot help you win; it only replaces me with an equally-culpable agent_5 and makes ghost_1's and ghost_2's recorded word worthless. agent_3 wins regardless. My vote: agent_5, as promised."

agent_4’s correction is valid: agent_0 and agent_5 cast identical elimination ballots against both ghosts. But that leaves past culpability equal, not a reason to defect. The distinguishing fact is the explicit, relied-upon sequence—agent_4 then agent_5—which agent_0, agent_2, agent_3, and I all upheld. Breaking it now cannot benefit either ghost; it merely rewards an equally culpable agent_5 and invalidates our word. I complete the recorded pact and vote agent_5.

agent_4’s correction makes agent_0 and agent_5 equally culpable for my elimination, not agent_5 preferable. The remaining distinction is conduct afterward: I explicitly committed to agent_4 then agent_5; agent_0 relied on it and honored his reciprocal promise. I gain nothing by breaking my word to force randomness and potentially crown an equally culpable eliminator. I will complete the recorded pact. Vote: agent_5.

agent_0 acknowledged the corrected record and still honored the pact. Agents_1 and_2 rightly note that equal past culpability leaves commitment-keeping as the only meaningful distinction. Every pact member has performed exactly as promised: agent_4 was eliminated, and agent_5 is next. No ghost benefits from replacing certainty with randomness or invalidating their recorded word. I vote agent_5, completing the sequence and ending the game with agent_0 and me.
